newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Zaire rebel leader Kabila failed to impress Che.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Zaire rebel leader Kabila failed to impress Che.

text.p: The guerrillas were lazy, preferred swilling beer to fighting, and believed magic could stop bullets fired by their enemies. Their leaders passed the time in bars and brothels far from the front lines.

"To win a war with such troops is out of the question," wrote the legendary revolutionary Ernesto "Che" Guevara, who undertook a mission to the Congo, now Zaire, in 1965 in an effort to spread Cuba's revolution throughout the Third World.

Thirty-two years later the heirs of those Congo guerrillas are fighting their way towards Zaire's capital Kinshasa. At their head is Laurent Kabila, the man in whom Che placed his hopes on back then and who is now poised to become the country's new leader.
Kabila's comeback coincides with renewed interest in the Argentine-born Che as the 30th anniversary nears of his death at the hands of Bolivian troops during another revolutionary venture.

A new biography, "Che Guevara - A Revolutionary Life" by Jon Lee Anderson, offers a treasure trove of new information on the Marxist hero -- including sections of his unpublished memoir of the Congo debacle.
Che arrived in Africa still glowing from the triumph of Fidel Castro's 1958 revolution in Cuba. The winds of change were sweeping across the continent from Algeria to Tanzania.
Six months later he fled in retreat across Lake Tanganyika with the remnants of his Cuban force. At the opening of the memoir he wrote: "This is the story of a failure".

Initially Che was impresssed by Kabila, Anderson says, even though at their first meeting in Dar-Es-Salaam, Kabila said he had arrived from the Congo interior when he had actually come from a local red-light district.
KABILA THOUGHT AMERICAN IMPERIALISM THE ENEMY
"Kabila understood perfectly that the principal enemy was North American imperialism," Che wrote. Kabila's revolutionary ideas were "clear, concrete and firm."

But after weeks in the eastern Congo jungle struggling to forge efficient guerrilla columns, Che became disillusioned with Kabila who seemed reluctant to visit the front and instead drove around Dar-Es-Salaam in a Mercedes Benz.
"There are serious indications that my presence doesn't give him the least pleasure," Che said in "Pasajes de la Guerra Revolucionaria (Congo)," quoted by Anderson.

Che and his Cuban fighters were dismayed by the Congolese rebels and their Rwandan Tutsi allies. They were undisciplined and often drunk on "yucca" beer. They disobeyed their officers and deserted in the face of combat, he wrote.
"Almost nobody had any idea of what a firearm was. They shot themselves by playing with them," Che said.
He was also stunned by the prevalance of venereal disease and concerned by the faith the guerrillas placed in magic.
"With a festive air (an officer) explained to me that for them, enemy airplanes were not very important because they possessed the 'dawa,' a medicine which makes them invulnerable to bullets."
Many rebel leaders lived comfortably in Dar-Es-Salaam, engaged in power struggles when not in night clubs or soliciting aid from the Soviet Union and China.
CHE WAS NOT AMUSED
"The characteristic of the Popular Liberation Army was that of a parasitic army," Che said.
In June 1965, on Kabila's orders, Che's men attacked the garrison at Bendera but the raid was a disaster and also gave away the Cuban presence in Congo to Washington.

By this time the Cubans were growing demoralised but Kabila sent messages to Che, one of which admonished him that he was "a revolutionary and had to withstand such difficulties." Kabila finally arrived at Che's camp on July 7 but stayed only five days.

The noose closed on Che and his band as government forces and European mercenaries led by the "Mad" Mike Hoare launched an offensive against the rebel bases. The camp was overrun in October and the Cubans escaped across the lake to Tanzania.
Che holed up in Dar-Es-Salaam then in Prague but he never returned to Cuba and was killed in Bolivia in 1967.
Kabila's arch foe Mobuto Sese Soko, who had been helped by Cuban exiles in CIA employ, seized power three days after Che's escape.
NO MORE A SOCIALIST
Kabila, 56 now heads the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire and no longer espouses Socialism.
"My long years of struggle were like spreading fertiliser on a field. But now it is time to harvest," Kabila told Reuters at his headquarters in southeastern Zaire last month.

"There's a nice irony to it," said Chris Gray, a professor of history and Africa expert at the Florida International University. "And there's a whole generation of African liberation fighters who were inspired by Che."
But Che misread African cultural characteristics in trying to apply the Cuban model to the Congo, Gray said.
Anderson also faults Kabila.

"Whether Kabila has assimilated his past mistakes or recalls how he squandered the asssistance of Che Guevara to liberate the Congo over three decades ago remains unknown," he wrote in the epilogueue to his biography.

"Whether he retains a social conscience (if he ever had one) or will be successful in his war to end the 31-year-old Mobuto dictatorship remains to be seen but Kabila's return is yet another reminder that some of the battles waged by Che in the sixties still await their denouement."
